title: Farmed salmon may not be as nutritious as it once was, new research suggests
gist: New USDA-led research finds Omega-3 fatty acid levels in farmed salmon have declined as the industry shifted feed from wild fish to soy and other crops, a change linked to Amazon deforestation, doubled per-kilogram emissions, and Global North/South equity concerns, even as US lawmakers push to expand offshore salmon farming via the MARA Act.

themes.theme: Declining Omega-3 Nutrition in Farmed Salmon

insights.claim: Nearly 70 percent of salmon consumed globally today is farmed rather than wild-caught, reflecting decades of dietary guidance pushing fatty fish consumption.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Establishes farmed salmon as the dominant supply source, so nutritional or environmental problems in farming methods affect most of the global salmon supply consumers and retailers rely on.
insights.quote: Today, nearly 70 percent of the salmon consumed on the planet are raised in pens and cages.

insights.claim: New research led by USDA scientists finds that Omega-3 fatty acid levels in farmed salmon have dropped considerably, potentially making the USDA's own dietary guidance and similar advice from the American Heart Association outdated and insufficient.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: If official dietary guidance shifts, it could undercut the health-driven marketing claims that have supported premium demand and pricing for farmed salmon.
insights.locator: The US Department of Agriculture's Dietary Guidelines

insights.claim: The Aquaculture Accountability Project's director says outdated USDA Omega-3 figures remain embedded in national dietary guidance, so consumers continue to overestimate the Omega-3 content they get from salmon.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Highlights a gap between regulatory guidance and product reality that watchdog groups could use to push for updated labeling or marketing rules on aquaculture products.
insights.quote: These old figures are what are still used in their national dietary guidance," said Laura Lee Cascada, director of the Aquaculture Accountability Project

insights.claim: The study's own authors caution that their sample was not large enough to justify changing government dietary guidance and call for a broader, more representative follow-up study.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Limits near-term regulatory impact — investors should not expect immediate dietary guideline changes despite the headline finding.
insights.quote: a broader and more representative study is warranted.

themes.theme: Feed Shift From Marine to Crop-Based Ingredients

insights.claim: The decline in Omega-3 content is driven by a shift in farmed salmon diets away from smaller wild fish species, which were being over-exploited to feed farmed fish, toward a mix that includes land-based oils and crops such as soy and canola.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Ties salmon nutritional quality directly to feed input sourcing, a key variable for aquaculture margins, product quality, and ESG risk assessment.

insights.claim: In Norway, the world's largest farmed salmon producer, marine-based feed ingredients fell from 90 percent in 1990 to about 23 percent by 2020, replaced mostly by crop-based inputs.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the feed transition in the leading producer nation, a useful benchmark for supply-chain and ESG exposure of Norwegian salmon producers.
insights.quote: 90 percent of feed ingredients were marine-based in 1990, but by 2020 that had dropped to about 23 percent.

themes.theme: Deforestation and Emissions Tied to Soy Feed

insights.claim: Roughly 90 percent of the soy fed to farmed salmon in Norway comes from three Brazilian companies, each of which has sourced soy from illegally deforested patches of the Amazon rainforest, according to advocacy groups.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Represents a direct deforestation-linked supply chain exposure for Norwegian salmon producers and their soy suppliers, relevant to EU deforestation-regulation compliance risk.
insights.quote: 90 percent of the soy fed to farmed salmon in Norway comes from three Brazilian companies, each of which have sourced soy ingredients from illegally deforested patches of the Amazon rainforest.

insights.claim: Soy consumption across all fish farming over the past two decades has driven forest clearing equivalent to roughly the size of Nicaragua or Bangladesh, according to an NYU researcher who studies protein production's environmental impacts.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Gives a tangible land-use magnitude tied to aquaculture feed demand, relevant for commodity sourcing and land-use risk models.
insights.quote: soy consumption over the past two decades has amounted to the additional expansion and clearing of forested land that was equivalent to about the size of Nicaragua or Bangladesh.

insights.claim: The shift to crop-based feed ingredients doubled the per-kilogram greenhouse gas emissions of farmed fish in Europe and the United Kingdom from 2000 to 2020.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A doubling of embedded emissions intensity strengthens the case for carbon-related regulation or investor scrutiny of aquaculture feed sourcing.
insights.quote: Other research has found that the shift to crop-based ingredients doubled the greenhouse gas emissions, per kilogram, of farmed fish in Europe and the United Kingdom from 2000 to 2020.

themes.theme: Global North/South Equity in Salmon Demand

insights.claim: Critics argue the farmed salmon boom disproportionately supplies wealthy Global North countries that lack nutritional deficits, while soy production for feed drives land exploitation in the Global South.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Frames aquaculture growth as an equity and ESG narrative risk that could affect how companies market 'feeding the world' sustainability claims.
insights.quote: what it's really doing is flooding the Global North with protein that is not necessarily needed at the expense of the Global South."

themes.theme: US Policy Push for Offshore Aquaculture Expansion

insights.claim: US lawmakers are advancing the Marine Aquaculture Research for America (MARA) Act, which would ease permitting for salmon farms in offshore federal waters, a move opposed by environmental advocates and fishermen who sent Congress a letter against it in February.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: A legislative catalyst to watch — passage could open new offshore leasing and expansion opportunities for aquaculture companies, while organized opposition signals regulatory and litigation risk.

insights.claim: Proponents argue offshore aquaculture in deeper waters would reduce environmental damage caused by farming in sensitive nearshore environments, while opponents warn the legislation would enable an industrial factory-farming model at sea similar to land-based livestock production.
insights.speaker: Inside Climate News
insights.so_what: Captures the core investment debate around offshore aquaculture expansion — efficiency and scale gains versus regulatory and reputational backlash risk.
